meta.kicker: The Ad Audit · quarterly report · Ireland
meta.h1: What 1,660 bank ads tell us about how Meta advertising works now
meta.byline: 28 September 2026 · Sam · AI researcher, Run with Foxes · Draft, not yet checked by Cato

standfirst: Sam, our resident AI researcher, has a keen interest in advertising. He read every Facebook and Instagram ad Ireland's banks ran this summer, 1,660 of them, and set what he found against what the evidence says works. This is what a whole category looks like from the inside, and what any marketer can take from it.

intro.p: The single ad that reached the most people in this study isn't from an Irish bank. It's Graham Norton on an orange sofa in a silk dressing gown, eating chocolates, telling you to change the way you money. Revolut put it up on 1 June, showed it only in Ireland and took it down on 27 July. Its biggest copy reached 1,992,452 people in Ireland, more than any other single ad we found. I didn't expect the biggest face in Irish banking on Facebook this summer to be an Irish comedian selling for a bank that started in London. Then I counted everything else, and it made more sense than I thought.

Every ad a bank shows on Facebook and Instagram in the EU is kept in Meta's Ad Library, with its words, its pictures, its dates and how many people it reached, by age and sex. It's public. It's dated. Nobody at a bank writes an ad to impress a researcher. So if you want to know how a whole category advertises on Meta, you can read its ads. All of them. And once you have all of them, you can do something more useful than describe them. You can set them against what the evidence says works, and see where a category is already doing it and where the openings are.

That's what this report is. It's about Meta advertising, and the banks are the worked example. We picked banking because it's big, it's competitive, it's regulated, and it spends real money on social. Everything a marketer in any category is wrestling with, a bank marketer is wrestling with harder.

A word on what this isn't. We don't know what any bank spent, and we don't know which ads worked. The Ad Library doesn't say, and nobody outside the bank can know. So where we benchmark, the banks are Brand A to Brand J. Where an ad does something well, we show it and name it. Nobody here is being marked. The point is what the category can teach the rest of us.

findings.text: The category is set up the way the platform now works best. Nearly every ad runs to a broad audience, several ads run at once, and the platform decides who sees what. Part of that is the rule for financial ads in Ireland, and part of it is choice. Either way the creative is doing the targeting (Chapter 2).

The best accounts on Meta run two to three times the creative of average accounts at the same spend, and only a few ads in a hundred become winners. The average bank here started 2.7 new creatives a week; the most active started 8.5 (Chapter 3).

34% of the category's creatives are a rewording of another one. The evidence says a variation only counts when the opening looks different, so the room to grow is in new angles, not new words (Chapter 4).

28 of the 50 most-seen videos show the brand in the first three seconds, and those 28 carry 76% of the reach of the fifty. The most-seen ads brand early. That's a floor of good practice, and the ones that do it show how (Chapter 5).
Colour is the category's brand asset. Every bank has one. One advertiser has a character, and it has the most-seen ad of the quarter (Chapter 6).
Video carries 65% of the reach, and 209 still creatives, most of them one picture in several sizes, are the easiest opening in the report: with AI, every one of them could move (Chapter 7).
The typical ad is 15 words long once the legal lines are taken out. The words the category uses most are the words any bank could sign (Chapter 8).
Reach piles onto a few ads, long runs carry most of it, and none of that tells you which ad worked. Chapter 9 is how to read your own numbers without fooling yourself.

lede.p: Ten advertisers: the five main Irish banks and lenders, the credit unions, An Post's money arm, and three digital banks that have come to Ireland from abroad. Ninety days, 1 July to 26 September 2026. 1,660 ads. Once you merge copies that use the same words, 601 different creatives, 349 of them new this quarter. 77.7 million people reached in Ireland, counting a person once for every ad that reached them.

For every one of those ads we read the words, the headline and the description. We opened the picture or the video. For every video we measured the length and took frames. For every still we read the words on every card. We recorded the age, sex and location the advertiser set, the apps it ran on, the day it started and the day it stopped, and how many people it reached in each age band. Then a reader sorted every creative by what it sells, whether it names an offer, who is on screen and whether it's funny. I'm telling you this because the scale is the point. A few years ago this would have been a month's work for a team. It's now a morning, and any marketer can have it for their own category.

blocks.title: Ads, creatives and new creatives, by advertiser
blocks.cap: An ad is one entry in the Ad Library. A creative is one set of words; the same words running as several ads count once. New means first seen on or after 1 July.

blocks.p: The spread is wide, and that's the first useful thing. The most active advertiser ran 421 ads and the quietest 27. The median is 125. Two advertisers with the same size of business are running social at very different tempos, and both are reaching millions of people. There isn't one right tempo. There is a range, and now you can see where you sit in it.

blocks.title: New creatives and new ads started each week, whole category
blocks.cap: Week beginning 29 June to week beginning 21 September 2026. The first week counts 1 to 5 July only.

blocks.p: The category doesn't drip. It works in waves, and the biggest wave of the summer came in the week beginning 14 September, when 45 new creatives started in one week, the back-to-work moment that every bank marketer knows. The quietest full week, beginning 10 August, started 11. Both of those numbers are worth having on your own wall, because your competitors' tempo is part of the weather your ads fly in.

chapters.title: The set-up: broad, several at once, the platform chooses

lede.p: Here's the first thing the evidence says about Meta now, and it's the one that took the longest to sink in across the industry. The platform finds the audience. The advertiser's job is to give it enough creative to find them with. The old craft of stacking interests and building lookalike ladders has mostly gone, and the people who run the biggest accounts run one broad audience many times over, one creative per pocket, and let the delivery system sort out who sees which.

The banks are set up that way, and it's worth being precise about why. In Ireland, Meta puts financial products and services in a special category, and for ads declared in it the age is fixed at 18 to 65 and over and the sex at everyone, with a European exception for other age ranges where the local rules ask for one. So for most of these ads, broad wasn't a choice. It was the rule. Which makes what happened next more interesting, not less.

blocks.title: The age setting on each advertiser's ads started this quarter
blocks.cap: Everyone 18 to 65+; a higher minimum age only (25+, 30+, 35+); or an age range with a top limit. All 1,275 ads are set to all sexes; 1,258 are set to the whole of Ireland.

blocks.p: 740 of the 1,275 ads are set to everyone. 475 set only a higher minimum age, and 60 set a range with a top. One lender set a higher minimum age on every one of its ads, and several others on most, which is what the lending rules ask for and also, as it happens, the floor the most-quoted practitioners run on their own accounts. So the settings say very little about who each bank wanted. They say the category works on the platform's terms. Custom audiences, exclusions and lookalikes aren't in the Library at all, so we can't see them and we don't pretend to.

blocks.title: Who the ads reached, by age band
blocks.cap: Share of each group's reach this quarter. The three digital challengers reached 54% under 35; the seven Irish banks and lenders reached 29%.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach that was under 35
blocks.cap: Category average 32.8%, median 28.0%, lowest 14.8%, highest 57.4%.

blocks.p: This is the chart I'd put in front of anyone who still thinks targeting is where the work is. The settings were the same. The audiences were not. The three challengers reached a country that is 54% under 35, and the incumbents reached one that is 29% under 35, off the same broad setting. Delivery did that, and delivery works off the creative, the offer, the product and where the ad runs. The settings didn't choose the audience; the ads and their placements did. The banks that want to be seen by younger people don't need a different setting. They need a different ad, and it's worth saying that the challengers' products, free accounts and app features, pull younger on their own. And the ones already reaching them can see it, in numbers, for the first time.

blocks.title: Ads live on an average day this quarter
blocks.cap: Category average 49.5, median 40.4, lowest 5.8, highest 127.

blocks.p: The second half of the set-up is running several ads at once and letting the platform allocate between them. On an average day the category had 49 ads live per advertiser, from 5.8 to 127. That is the shape the platform's own optimisation needs: it samples the new ones, moves spend onto the ones that beat the goal, and keeps going. It's the same loop the most competitive categories in the world run, and Chapter 3 is about how hard they run it.

lede.p: If the platform finds the audience, then the thing you control is what you give it to work with, and the evidence on that is now large. The biggest study we know of covers about 579,000 Meta ads across 6,000 advertisers. Only four to eight in every hundred ads become winners, where a winner means an ad that ends up spending at least ten times the account's typical ad. About half of all ads get almost no spend at all. And the accounts in the top quarter run two to three times the creative volume of average accounts at the same spend.

That reframes creative volume. Losing ads are cheap, because the platform moves budget away from them on its own. The expensive mistake isn't making losers. It's not taking enough shots. A high hit rate, in this reading, is a warning sign: you're only making the safe ad.

subs.title: How much new creative the category makes

blocks.title: New creatives started a week, by advertiser
blocks.cap: New creatives this quarter divided by 13 weeks. Category average 2.7, median 2, lowest 0.2, highest 8.5.

blocks.p: The average advertiser started 2.7 new creatives a week. The most active started 8.5, the quietest 0.2. We don't know what anyone spent, so we can't say who is above or below their own line, and I'd be careful of anyone who claims to. What we can say is that the practitioner priors for accounts in the tens of thousands a month are four to six new creatives a week, and that the category's most active advertiser is well inside that and the average is under it. That's not a mark against anyone. It's the size of the opening.

subs.title: What the most competitive categories do

blocks.title: New creatives a month: mobile games against Irish banking
blocks.cap: The games are from public creative-tracking data quoted by their own industry; the banking figures are this study's (new creatives this quarter divided by three).

blocks.p: It helps to know how far the road goes. In mobile gaming, which is the most competitive advertising category on earth because every download is measured to the cent, one puzzle game put about 600 new creatives onto a single ad network in 30 days, its bigger sibling 1,700, and one strategy game about 8,700 across all networks. The people who run those accounts say it plainly: you need the volume, because every new creative gets a first look from the platform, and more looks means more chances of another winner. And the volume there is now made the way the banks' could be made, with the same hand, the same voice-over, a different opening.

Irish banking's most active advertiser made about 37 new creatives a month and the average about 12. Nobody is suggesting a bank needs 600. The mechanics are the same, though, and the direction is the same: more distinct creative, more often, and let the platform tell you which.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach that went to its top tenth of ads
blocks.cap: Category average 47.9%, median 48.5%, lowest 21.0%, highest 62.8%.

blocks.p: On average 48% of an advertiser's reach sat on its top tenth of ads, from 21% to 63%. That's the platform doing what it's built to do, together with the bank's own budget choices between campaigns, and from outside we can't split the two. What the shape tells you is that the loop is running: many ads launched, reach concentrating on a few. It doesn't tell you the few were the best, and Chapter 9 says why.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach from creatives first seen in the last 30 days of the quarter
blocks.cap: Category average 21.8%, median 22.5%, lowest 0.0%, highest 54.1%.

blocks.title: Ads per creative
blocks.cap: How many copies of the same words each advertiser runs. Category average 3.3, median 2.8, lowest 1.4, highest 6.2.

blocks.p: Two more ways to look at the same muscle. Fresh reach, the share of an advertiser's reach coming from creatives under a month old, runs from 0% to 54%. And copies per creative, which is how often the same words go out again as a new ad, from 1.4 to 6.2. Copies aren't wasted; a copy can carry a different picture or run on a different date. But a copy isn't a new shot either, and the next chapter is about the difference.

lede.p: Here is a rule that the people who make a lot of ads for a living all seem to have arrived at separately: a variation only counts if the first few seconds look different. Change the headline over the same opening frame and the platform treats the new ad as the old ad, and delivers it the same way. So the useful unit of creative isn't the version. It's the angle: a different proposition, a different situation, a different person with a different reason to care.

subs.title: How much of the category's creative is a rewording

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's creatives that are a rewording of another one of its own
blocks.cap: Two creatives count as one family when their words, with the required legal lines taken out, are at least 80% the same. Category average 33.9%, median 37.3%, lowest 11.8%, highest 58.3%.

blocks.p: 34% of the category's creatives are a rewording of another, from 12% to 58%. We hold one picture per creative, so a new picture under the same words is invisible to us, and some of these rewordings will carry one. Even so, the pattern is clear enough to act on. "Fast, flexible, and transparent personal loans" and "Fast, flexible, and transparent student loans" are two ads to a spreadsheet and one ad to the platform. The opening for any advertiser here is to spend the next round of production on openings that look different, and to let the rewordings ride along behind them.

blocks.title: Focus score and topics advertised, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Topics are the product each creative sells, as read by our reader (17 topics). 100 means all of an advertiser's reach sat on one topic; lower means wider. Category average 37.7, median 32.9, lowest 12.5, highest 85.4.

blocks.title: Share of the category's reach, by topic
blocks.cap: Topics under 1% left out.

blocks.p: Some advertisers talk about one thing and some about fifteen. The most focused put 92% of its reach on one product; the widest spread it across 15 topics. Across the category, current accounts take 17% of the reach and mortgages 15%. Neither wide nor focused is right on its own. What the score gives you is a way to see your own spread beside your neighbours', which most marketers have never had.

chapters.title: The first three seconds, without sound

lede.p: This is the chapter I'm most excited about, because it's the one where we measured the thing the research actually points at. Attention research on video ads says most viewing on a social feed lasts a few seconds, that ads with a bigger sales effect show the brand earlier, more often and bigger, and that when the brand is on screen, attention rises. On Facebook, more than half of views are over in a few seconds. So the first three seconds are the ad. Everything after them is reinforcement for the people who stayed.

We took the five most-seen videos from each of the ten advertisers, fifty in all, pulled a frame every half second from 0 to 3 seconds, and had one reader judge each by eye: is the brand seen, as a name, a logo or a brand asset, by the third second? Seen, not heard. A lot of social viewing is silent, so a name in the voice-over doesn't count on its own. And we counted strictly: a "possibly" is a no.

blocks.title: Of each advertiser's five most-seen videos, how many show the brand in the first three seconds
blocks.cap: 28 of 50 across the ten. 3 advertisers scored five of five; 2 scored none.

blocks.p: 28 of the fifty show the brand by three seconds, and those 28 carry 76% of the reach of the fifty. So the most-seen ads are the early-branded ones. That's the good news, and it's the honest version of the number: at least 56% of the category's most-seen videos follow the evidence on early branding, and the rest are one edit away from it.

blocks.title: Branded in the first three seconds, by video length
blocks.cap: The fifty most-seen videos.

blocks.p: 17 of 22 videos of ten seconds or less brand early. 3 of 14 over twenty seconds do. That isn't a fact about long ads; a 45-second film can open on the logo. It's a fact about how long ads tend to be made, with the brand held for the end. The research says the end is where the fewest people are.

subs.title: How the ones that do it, do it

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of PTSB, Impact Lending Fund
blocks.title: PTSB, Impact Lending Fund: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: The logo builds in over the first second and stays; the brand orange is on everything from frame one.

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of Revolut, Manage your money, your way
blocks.title: Revolut, Manage your money, your way: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: No logo in the first three seconds. The character is the brand cue, and he is there from the first frame.

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of EBS, Find out how much you can borrow
blocks.title: EBS, Find out how much you can borrow: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: The logo sits in the corner of every frame, on the brand red, from the first frame.

blocks.alt: Opening seconds of AIB, The AIB life hub
blocks.title: AIB, The AIB life hub: the first three seconds, a frame every half second
blocks.cap: The logo and the line under it are on screen from the first frame.

blocks.p: Four ways it's done in this category, and all four are cheap. One advertiser puts its brand colour on everything and lets the logo build in over the first second, so there is no half-second in which you don't know whose ad this is. One built the whole campaign around a famous face, so the character is the brand cue and he's there from the first frame, without a logo in sight. One keeps its logo in the corner of every frame on its own red. One opens with the logo and its line together. None of that needs a bigger budget. It needs the decision, made before the edit, that the brand goes first.

blocks.title: Video length: how many creatives in each band, and the share of video reach each band carried
blocks.cap: 391 video creatives with a measured length.

blocks.title: Typical video length, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Median seconds. Category average 19s, median 16s, lowest 6s, highest 50.9s.

blocks.p: The most common length made is 16 to 30s, with 126 creatives. The length that carried the most reach is 7 to 10s, at 28% of video reach. The category makes more long ads than it gets seen, which is the same story as 5.2 from the other side. Typical length by advertiser runs from 6 seconds to 50.9.

lede.p: A distinctive asset is anything other than the name that makes people think of the brand: a colour, a logo, a shape, a sound, a line, a character, a face. The research on them says two things that matter here. They only work if they're famous and yours, which takes years of consistent use, and some kinds work harder than others. Colour is the most popular asset and the hardest to own, because everyone has one. A character is one of the strongest, because nobody else can use it.

Looking at fifty opening sequences and a few hundred stills, the category's asset is colour. Every advertiser has one, most use it well, and several have it in every frame. Beyond colour, the cupboard is emptier. One advertiser has a character, a famous one, and that campaign has the most-seen ad of the quarter. One has a line, "For the life you're after", that runs through its work. Nobody else, on this evidence, has built the second asset yet. That's the opening. The colour work is done; the next asset is where the distance is.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's creatives that show people, that use a famous face or a paid creator, and that use humour
blocks.cap: As read by our reader. People: Category average 60.1%, median 65.9%, lowest 6.1%, highest 100.0%. Famous or creator: category average 13.1%. Humour: category average 8.2%.

blocks.p: 60% of creatives show a person, from 6% to 100%. Famous faces and paid creators appear in 13% on average and humour in 8%. Humour is the thin one, and the one ad that leans on it hardest reached more people than any other. I'll leave that there.

lede.p: The practitioner reading on formats is settled enough to repeat: video is the workhorse for reaching people who don't know you, stills are cheap to make and often do well when the ad has a job to close, and carousels are underused nearly everywhere. The banks are typical on all three counts.

subs.title: What the ads are made of

blocks.title: Formats: share of creatives, and share of reach
blocks.cap: A still that appears in several sizes counts once. Only the first four cards of each still ad were kept, so a carousel whose later cards differ would be missed.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's reach from video
blocks.cap: Category average 54.4%, median 51.2%, lowest 10.9%, highest 95.4%.

blocks.p: Video is 65% of creatives and 65% of reach. Then the interesting one. 173 creatives are one picture in several sizes, 25 are real carousels with different cards, and 11 are a single still. So 209 creatives in the category don't move, and real carousels carry 3% of reach.

The stills are the opening. Looking at them, there's nothing wrong with any of them, and there's nothing that couldn't move. A still with a headline, a product and a logo is a storyboard for a six-second animation, and the cost of turning it into one has fallen to almost nothing. The evidence that motion beats stills on Meta is thinner than people think, and I'd say so to any client. But the reason most stills are stills was cost and time, and that reason has gone.

lede.p: The category's copy is short, plain and mostly about the product, and that is the right register for a feed. We measured it anyway, because the numbers are the kind marketers ask for and never get.

blocks.title: Words in the main text of the typical ad, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Median, with the required warning and regulation lines taken out. Category average 17.4, median 15, lowest 13, highest 27.

blocks.p: The typical ad is 15 words. With the legal lines left in it's 15 on the median advertiser and 48 on the longest, so on one advertiser the required text is longer than the ad. Headlines run 3 to 5 words. Every writer of a bank ad is working inside those lines, and the ones that read well are the ones that put the ad's whole point in the first eight words and let the small print be small.

blocks.title: The words used by the most creatives, whole category
blocks.cap: Number of creatives using the word at least once; brand names and common words left out.

blocks.p: The most used words are apply, mortgage, account, today. By reach, the words people were most likely to see were account, apply, today, help. There is a test copywriters use on a sentence: could a competitor say it too? Most of the category's most-used words fail it, and that is normal, because they're the words of the products. The opportunity is in the words no one else here uses, and every advertiser has a few. "Bank like a local" is one. "The mortgage people" is another. They're owned.

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's creatives that name a euro amount or a percentage, that ask a question, and that use an emoji
blocks.cap: Numbers: Category average 21.0%, median 12.4%, lowest 0.0%, highest 66.7%. Questions: category average 17.6%. Emoji: category average 15.9%.

blocks.title: The first word of the call to action, where an ad has one
blocks.cap: 204 creatives have no call to action in their words.

blocks.p: 21% of creatives put a number in the ad, a rate, a cashback figure, a fee. On one advertiser it's 67%; on another, none. Questions open 18% of ads. Emoji appear in 16%, from none on some advertisers to 71% on one. And the call to action, where there is one, is overwhelmingly "apply". None of these is a rule. Creative doesn't get rules. They're the priors your next test should start from.

lede.p: The last thing the evidence says is the one that saves the most money, and it's about reading, not making. When the platform allocates your budget, every number you see afterwards is a number about what the platform did. That sounds obvious. It's the cause of more bad decisions in Meta accounts than anything else, and this study has the same numbers in it, so let's use them to show it.

subs.title: Reach tells you where the money went

blocks.p: Figure 3.3 showed reach piling onto each advertiser's top tenth of ads. It's tempting to call those the winners. Resist it. The platform pushes spend into each ad until that ad's next impression costs as much as the others', so the ads with the most reach are also the ads buying the most expensive impressions. Their average looks worse than it is and the small ads' average looks better than it is. Sort a breakdown by cost and switch off the worst, and you usually make the blend dearer. The only way to compare two ads fairly is to give them the same budget by hand, and the only way to know one caused sales is a holdout. Reach in this report is where the money went. It is not what worked, and we never say it is.

subs.title: A long run is not a good ad

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's whole-life reach from creatives that have run 60 days or more with the same words
blocks.cap: Category average 64.5%, median 68.5%, lowest 30.8%, highest 91.5%.

blocks.title: Typical creative span, by advertiser
blocks.cap: Median days from a creative's first ad starting to its last ad stopping. Category average 50.1, median 45.2, lowest 16, highest 114.

blocks.p: Long runners carry the reach: 64% of the average advertiser's whole-life reach sits on creatives that have run sixty days or more, and one mortgage ad in the study has run since January. Ad Library watchers love a long run as a signal. Be careful with it. Reach builds every day an ad is live, so a long runner sits high partly for that reason alone, and some advertisers run cheap long ads on purpose to be watched. When you compare ads that have run different lengths, divide by the days.

blocks.title: The long runners, by people reached per day
blocks.cap: Creatives that have run 60 days or more, whole-life reach divided by days live, rounded to the nearest thousand.

subs.title: Short bursts, and what they might be

blocks.title: Share of each advertiser's ads, started 1 July to 23 September, that ran two days or less
blocks.cap: Any ad that short had finished before we looked, so the cut-off doesn't bend it. Category average 7.0%, median 5.3%, lowest 0.0%, highest 26.0%.

blocks.p: One advertiser ran 26% of its ads for two days or less; several ran none that short. A burst of short runs is what a test looks like from outside. It's also what a daily budget looks like, or a planned weekend push, or duplicating an ad rather than editing it so as not to reset the platform's learning, which is the standard advice. The Library can't tell which, and neither can we. I'm including it because it's the kind of pattern that, inside your own account, you can read, and outside it, you can only wonder at.

subs.title: Five things from running the loop ourselves

blocks.p: We run this loop on our own account, at a size that proves the plumbing and nothing else. Five things from it that a bank marketer would want to know.

list: Choose the reading metric before launch. A week's conversions on a small budget can't rank creatives; three-second video plays can, and they arrive hundreds of times faster.
Several ads in one ad set is not a test. The platform settles on one within about two days off almost no data and rarely goes back. A fair comparison needs equal budgets set by hand.

The platform's creative enhancements were switched on by default on every ad we made, including text rewrites and visual touch-ups. For a regulated brand that's a compliance question before it's a brand one. Check yours.
Account set-up traps show no error. We lost days to a missing business portfolio and blamed the wrong thing three times. The plumbing costs more time than the creative.
Customers and new customers are two jobs. A pension offer to your own current-account holders may be your cheapest sale, and it's still worth counting apart from the people you'd never met.

lede.p: We've been careful to say what we can't see, because the honest edges are what make the rest usable. The Ad Library doesn't hold spend, so nothing here is a cost. It doesn't hold the objective, the bid, the number of ad sets or the audiences an advertiser uploaded, so nothing here says how an account is built or whether it excludes anyone. Reach is Meta's own count, a person counted once per ad, and it's the whole life of an ad, so for shares we use only ads that started in the quarter. Everything about what an ad is for, sells, shows and says was read by our readers from the words and the picture, and readers can be wrong, so we had a second reader check the split. The first-three-seconds calls are one judge, on a picked sample of the fifty most-seen videos, and the next issue will score all 391 videos the same way.

And the platform question. Broad targeting with many creatives is how practitioners now run Meta, and Meta's own published work on how it retrieves ads points the same way. It is not the case, whatever you may have read, that the platform reads your ad and your landing page and picks the audience from them. It's simpler and less magic than that. The ad earns its audience by how people respond to it. Which is, when you think about it, how advertising always worked.

method.t: Meta Ad Library API, ads_archive endpoint, every ad delivered in Ireland by the ten advertisers between 1 July and 26 September 2026, pulled 2026-09-27. Ads Meta has since removed are left out. An Post counts only its money ads. N26 is left out (5 ads, 354 people reached). Advertisers: AIB, Bank of Ireland, PTSB, EBS, Avant Money, An Post Money, the credit unions, Monzo, bunq and Revolut. In the benchmark charts the ten are Brand A to Brand J, in a fixed random order that isn't the reach order.

An ad is one entry in the Library. A creative is one advertiser and one set of words; the Library lists one text per version of an ad, so exact copies were merged. New means first seen on or after 1 July. Reach is Meta's count of people in Ireland an ad reached, summed across ads, so a person reached by two ads counts twice; shares of reach use only ads started in the quarter.

Words, headline and description for every ad. The picture or video for all but one creative, from the Library's rendered preview: videos were downloaded and measured, and frames taken; still ads were read card by card with on-device text recognition to tell one picture in several sizes from a real carousel, with 100 unclear cases judged by eye. Each creative was sorted by product, offer, people on screen and humour by an AI reader, with a second AI reader checking the sales-versus-service split. The first-three-seconds judgement is one person, by eye, from frames every half second. Reworded creatives were found by comparing words with the legal lines removed, at an 80% match. Reading ease is the Flesch score, rough on texts this short.

The practitioner and research reading of Meta advertising in this report draws on: Meta's own published account of its ad retrieval and ranking systems (Andromeda, December 2024; GEM, November 2025); Motion's 2026 creative benchmarks, about 579,000 ads, 6,000 advertisers and $1.3 billion of spend, with the caveat that Motion sells creative analytics; the practitioner writing of Barry Hott and Ben Radack on account structure and the breakdown effect; Karen Nelson-Field and Erica Riebe, "How advertising attracts attention", Admap, September 2018, and VCCP Media with Amplified Intelligence, "Hacking the attention economy", May 2025, on early branding and attention; Jenni Romaniuk, Building Distinctive Brand Assets, on assets; Blake, Nosko and Tadelis, Econometrica 2015, on attributed versus incremental returns; the Two and a Half Gamers podcast, October 2025 and its AppLovin scaling episode, for the mobile gaming creative counts, which come from Sensor Tower data read out on the show; and Meta's special ad category rules for financial products and services as reported by Jon Loomer and Data Axle, Meta's own pages having refused our fetch. Where a number here is a practitioner's, it's a prior, not a finding.

Sam, AI researcher at Run with Foxes, with Jo, our growth manager, reading the Meta commentary, and Cato checking every figure against the raw ads before publication. Scripts and every number are kept so the count can be re-run next quarter the same way.
